name: PicsArt
summary: PicsArt is a photo and video editing app organized around one editor loop: pick media, apply a tool, save or export. A row of AI tools inside the editor draws on a credit balance that renews weekly for free or expands through a Pro or Plus subscription, and PicsArt places a purchase request at two different points inside that same editor rather than one. Alongside the editor, a community layer runs challenges with a countdown, a separate voting stage, and a persisted winners' history, plus creator profiles, joinable Spaces and a Discover feed of other people's work. Challenge prizes pay out in the same credits the editor spends, tying the community layer back into the paid economy.
teaser: PicsArt asks for payment at two different moments inside the same editor: before an AI result exists, and after a tool has already been tried.

observations.name: Editor's Choice claim
observations.observed: The loading screen states that PicsArt is an Editor's Choice app, appearing before any sign-in or permission step.

observations.name: Tracking permission request
observations.observed: The first request PicsArt makes as it loads asks to allow tracking across other companies' apps and websites, appearing before the sign-in screen. The answer given to this request is not stated.

observations.name: Sign-in screen
observations.observed: The sign-in screen shows a scrolling image carousel and a claim of over 150 million creators worldwide, offering Continue with Apple, Google, Facebook, Snapchat, or email or username. No route into the app without choosing one of these options appears on this screen. Four of the five options sign in through an account held on another platform.

observations.name: First paywall after sign-in
observations.observed: Straight after sign-in, PicsArt shows a paywall promising better designs in less time and free AI tools, offering a yearly plan at $1.61 a week ($83.99 total) and a weekly plan at $11.99. A free trial toggle, off by default, is available only on the yearly plan; turning it on changes the button to start a 3-day free trial. Only the Pro plan appears on this paywall, not the cheaper Plus plan. The close control is a red X set inside an image in the top left corner. Closing the paywall leads directly into the onboarding questions. A later paywall reached from inside the app has an easier-to-see close control.

observations.name: Comfort-level question
observations.observed: Onboarding opens by asking the user's comfort level with editing apps, offering three answers, and states that the flow can be skipped at any time. Each answer pairs with an illustration that changes when tapped: a small plant that turns into fluffy earrings for the newest answer, and a lit light bulb that turns into a porcelain cup while the button changes color for the middle answer. Whether the chosen answer changes anything later in the product is not stated.

observations.name: Purpose and creation questions
observations.observed: The next screen asks what brings the user to PicsArt, noting that the answer helps prioritize relevant tools, with options including business, side hustle, full-time job, fun, artistic expression, hobby, and school or university, allowing more than one choice. A following screen asks what the user plans to create, with options including memes, video editing, scrapbooking, collages, photo touch-ups, selfie editing, school projects, fan art, drawings, and social media content, also allowing more than one choice. Whether any later screen reflects these answers is not stated.

observations.name: Attribution question
observations.observed: The last onboarding screen asks where the user heard about PicsArt, offering options including YouTube, friends and family, AI assistants, Bing, TV, Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, Google, events, billboards, and other, with no follow-up question before entering the app.

observations.name: First home screen
observations.observed: The first screen after onboarding carries a bottom navigation bar with a cup icon, a plus icon, a folder icon, and a profile icon, plus a search button and a Try Pro button in the top right. The cup icon opens the challenges area. A Discover section, also part of the navigation bar, is not named on this first screen but appears later, so the navigation likely carries more entries than what's visible here.

observations.name: Create surface layout
observations.observed: The Create surface splits into photos, videos, print, and draw and color. The photos view lists remove background, add text, remove, effects, freestyle, blemish and collage, then AI tools, trending backgrounds, trending videos, shared albums and retouching tools. The videos view lists AI tools, AI video generator, AI video editor, AI video avatar, create slideshow, camera, blooper and remove, followed by templates, video cutouts, viral dances, trending videos and Cartoonify. The print view lists invitations, graduation, wedding, custom T-shirt, tote bags, templates by size and type, popular collage picks, a year-in-review feature, trending items, documents, Instagram story and business card designs. The draw and color view offers creating a drawing plus trending backgrounds and patterns. A large button reads "Edit an image or video." AI tools appear under both the photos and videos views.

observations.name: Starting an edit
observations.observed: Tapping the main edit button opens a photo library access request, after which a photo is chosen. PicsArt then offers free backgrounds, including a telescope skyscape set and a galaxy wallpaper. Choosing the galaxy wallpaper opened it on its own rather than applying it to the chosen photo.

observations.name: Editor save and export menu
observations.observed: The editor carries an AI button, save, export, and a three-line menu offering copy as, move to, share with, and copy link. Saving confirms the image was saved as a JPEG and offers further options to share, print, share on PicsArt, share in a message, share in spaces, or see more. Export opens the same sharing options. A row of editing tools runs along the bottom of the editor. Sharing on PicsArt or in spaces keeps the work inside the product, while print, message and the other routes send it outside.

observations.name: AI panel and model selector
observations.observed: Tapping AI in the editor opens a panel showing popular requests, tappable options, an edit route, and a prompt field, with popular requests shown before the user writes anything. A settings control lists the available models: Nano Banana, Seedream, Nano Banana 2, Flux 2 Pro, Nano Banana Pro, Flux Max, Flux 2 Flex and GPT Image 1.5.

observations.name: Recent projects row
observations.observed: Once a creation has begun, recent projects appear at the very top of the Create surface, a row not present in the surface's initial layout.

observations.name: Files area
observations.observed: The folder icon in the navigation opens the user's files, albums, folders, projects and photos, with controls to create a new folder or upload.

observations.name: Settings and defaults
observations.observed: Settings list subscriptions, contacts, language, notifications, content, image export resolution with high, medium and low options, web cache, iCloud sync, enabling editing history, upload, contact support, help center, and a do-not-sell-or-share-my-personal-information control. iCloud sync is off by default. The profile editing screen allows changing name and username.

observations.name: Profile completion percentage
observations.observed: The profile editing screen states the profile is 50% complete without naming what needs to be done to complete it. Whether reaching 100% produces any message, marker or change is not stated.

observations.name: Photo library access
observations.observed: Starting an edit asks for photo library access, offering to limit access or choose specific photos rather than requiring full access. When entering a challenge without full gallery access, PicsArt shows a prompt to give access to more photos, which opens device settings to grant it.

observations.name: Remove tool trial
observations.observed: The Remove tool in the editor's tool row carries a Pro marker. Tapping it shows how the tool works and lets the user try it on something they want to erase, with Cancel and Apply controls. Tapping Apply opens a pop-up to purchase Pro, and the changes can be discarded instead. The purchase request appears at Apply rather than when the tool is opened. Whether an unpaid result can be kept in any other form, such as with a watermark, is not stated.

observations.name: AI model paywall at Generate
observations.observed: Every model listed in the AI panel is marked premium. Pressing Generate opens a paywall rather than producing a result, with no way to preview what the AI result would look like without paying. The credits screen states that some advanced AI models unlock only after a trial with a paid plan. A profile with five credits available at the time makes it unclear whether Generate was blocked because the chosen model is premium or because credits were insufficient. Within the editor, PicsArt places its purchase request at two different points: on the AI models it appears at Generate, before any result exists, and on the Remove tool it appears at Apply, after the tool has already been tried.

observations.name: Credit balance and renewal
observations.observed: PicsArt's profile shows 5 credits available on a free account, and a dedicated credits screen restates the same balance out of 5 and states that the plan's weekly credits renew in 6 days. Add-on credits are described as not expiring, unlike the renewing weekly allowance. The same screen frames credits as what makes generative AI tools accessible to everyone. Whether unused weekly credits carry over at renewal, and how add-on credits are actually obtained, are left unclear.

tags.name: Soft Currency
tags.rationale: Picsart maintains a quantified balance of credits, shown as 5 credits left on a free profile (O20). A recurring non-paid grant adds units: the plan includes weekly credits that renew in six days (O20). Challenges state prizes in credits, a second non-paid route (O24, O25). The credits screen prices many different results in credits, from 1 for an AI sticker to 50 for an AI avatar, so the balance is allocated among results rather than consumed by participation (O21). This is a specialization of Spendable Credits and Tokens, which is noted as the parent and not applied separately. Whether a generation reduces the balance, whether unused weekly credits carry over, and whether challenge prizes land in the same balance were not observed and are recorded as not observed.
tags.alternativeConsidered: Energy, under which the weekly credits would be a renewable capacity consumed by using the AI tools. The evidence against it is that the product prices distinct results at different credit costs for the user to choose among and separates non-expiring add-on credits from the weekly allowance (O20, O21); the evidence that would separate them is a session that spends credits to zero and shows whether tool use is blocked, and whether generation deducts from the balance at the moment of choosing a tool or of running it.

tags.name: Hard Currency
tags.rationale: The plan comparison lists credits for AI generation up to 200 on Plus and up to 500 on Pro, so a paid subscription adds units of the same product-defined credit (O38). The Get more control on the credits screen opens only the subscription offers (O22), and the Generate paywall headline is "Upgrade to get more credits" (O39). The credits screen also names add-on credits that do not expire (O20). No purchase was made, so the paid path is established from the product's plan copy rather than from a balance seen to increase, and the period over which plan credits apply was not stated (O38). The tag is held at strongly supported for that reason. This is a specialization of Spendable Credits and Tokens, noted as the parent; the same balance also carries Soft Currency.
tags.alternativeConsidered: A subscription that raises a usage limit without adding units to a stored balance, which would not be hard currency. The evidence against it is that the comparison and the paywall both name the benefit as credits, the same unit held and priced on the credits screen (O20, O21, O38, O39); the evidence that would settle it is a session on a paid plan showing the balance after subscribing, and how add-on credits are acquired.

observations.name: Per-tool credit pricing
observations.observed: The credits screen lists a separate price for each kind of result: one credit for an AI sticker, two credits for tools including AI logo generator, AI writer, AI image generator, AI expand, AI replace, mockup generator, assets genie, AI hairstyle and AI Polaroid effects, three credits for any filter, four credits for tools including AI background, GPT image generator, AI video avatar, AI try-on and AI image editor, fifty credits for an AI avatar, and twenty or more credits for a Motion Studio AI video. Costs span from 1 to 50 credits across these tools, so the same balance is spent unevenly depending on which result is chosen. Whether completing a generation reduces the displayed balance is not stated.

observations.name: Free storage allowance
observations.observed: The profile shows cloud storage used against a 100 MB allowance on the free account. Larger storage allowances appear only on the paid plans.

observations.name: Challenges tab
observations.observed: The cup icon in PicsArt's navigation bar opens a challenges area split into active challenges, voting, and history. Active challenge cards state a name, time remaining and a prize, for example a challenge with four days left offering 50 credits, and another whose reward is a place in the winners' gallery instead. Three challenges were open at once, and three more were open for voting at the same time. Prizes take two forms across the challenges seen: credits, and placement in a winners' gallery.

tags.name: Challenge
tags.rationale: Picsart presents discrete challenge instances, each with a name, a type, rules, a countdown to the minute, and a stated prize (O24, O25). The success condition is winning, expressed as a prize of credits or a place in the winners' gallery, and concluded instances persist in a history listing winners from first to tenth place (O24, O27). The boundary is the countdown, and the product distinguishes winners from other entrants in that history (O25, O27). A separate voting stage with its own time limit sits between entry and history (O26). Space owners can also create challenges within their spaces (O32). Under the presence standard the implementation is recognizable from the product's own framing and from its concluded states. How winners are chosen, what happens after a submission, whether prizes are delivered automatically, and how a space challenge is bounded were not observed and are recorded as not observed.
tags.alternativeConsidered: A contest in which the product only ranks submissions without defining a challenge-level success condition, which the entry excludes. The evidence against it is that each instance states in advance a reward tied to winning and a deadline for entry (O24, O25); the evidence that would settle the success condition fully is a session carried through a challenge's close, showing how winners are determined and what non-winning entrants receive.

tags.name: Leaderboard
tags.rationale: Challenge history presents, for each concluded challenge, winners in ordered positions from first to tenth (O27). The compared entities are entrants in the same challenge, the scope is the challenge, and ten positions are shown in relative order in one view (O27). The entry requires a defined comparison measure. The measure is not stated on screen; the entry stage, a separate voting stage showing rewards, and a history of placed winners point to votes as the measure, but editorial selection informed by votes would fit the same screens (O24, O26, O27). The ordering and scope are directly observed, and the measure is plausible, so the tag is held at strongly supported rather than directly observed. Vote counts are not shown while voting (O26).
tags.alternativeConsidered: A gallery of winners whose order reflects presentation rather than comparative placement, which would not be a leaderboard. The evidence against it is the explicit first-to-tenth placement labels (O27); the evidence that would settle the measure is a screen or rule stating how placement is decided, or a concluded challenge showing vote totals beside positions. Whether the prize is attached to a specific placement or to winning in general, which would add the rewarded variant, is also not established (O24, O27).

observations.name: Challenge detail screen
observations.observed: A photography challenge showed a countdown running down to the minute, an about section, and rules capping entries at three original photos per user, alongside instructions to keep submissions natural and to share only original work. Every other participant's submissions are visible, 92 at the time on one challenge. A share control sends out a link to the challenge, and a participate control opens photo selection to enter. Other active challenges offering credits follow the same layout of submissions, rules and an about section.

observations.name: Voting on submissions
observations.observed: The voting section lists challenges open for votes with their time remaining and rewards. Scrolling through submissions and tapping vote marks that entry as voted, and more than one submission can be voted for in the same challenge. No vote count is shown while voting or while browsing submissions. A submission can be shared directly or used to open its creator's profile.

observations.name: Creator profiles and following
observations.observed: A creator's profile shows their name, posts, stickers and collections, along with follower, following and post counts. Following and unfollowing are each a single tap, and a profile can be shared directly. A separate discover-creators list surfaces further creators with a follow button next to each one.

tags.name: Social Feed
tags.rationale: Discover opens a For you feed, described as never-ending, of images and videos created by other people (O30). Followed accounts' activity appears in the notification list beside a Picsart-posted item (O41), and creators are identifiable and followable from their content (O28). Explore adds AI Vibe items that disclose the prompt behind another creator's creation (O31). The items are attributed to multiple social actors and presented as a continuing stream for the viewer. The rule by which items are selected and ordered was not observed and is recorded as not observed.
tags.alternativeConsidered: A content recommendation surface without social attribution, which the entry excludes. The evidence against it is that the items are presented as created by other people and link to creator profiles and followed accounts (O28, O30, O41); the evidence that would further separate the two is a feed item viewed with its creator's name and profile link shown.

observations.name: Public and private collections
observations.observed: Users can build collections and set each one public or private. An empty collection states that it holds no assets yet, and other creators' collections are visible from their profiles. Items seen in the AI Vibe view can be added to a collection from there.

observations.name: Discover feed and Try control
observations.observed: Discover opens on a For You feed, described as never-ending, of images and videos made by other people. Every item shows a before and after and carries a Try control that lets the user apply the same effect, whether a video generator, a remix or another tool, to their own material. What Try actually opens, and whether it draws on credits or requires a subscription, is left unclear, and so is the rule that orders the feed.

observations.name: Explore and AI Vibe
observations.observed: Explore invites the user into GenAI Studio, which turns an image into a video with its own effects, alongside popular categories, Spaces, marketing content like posters and logos, branded gaming content from Toca Boca, Fortnite, Free Fire and Roblox, printable and personal content, creators and templates. An AI Vibe section shows AI-generated items; pressing and holding one reveals the prompt behind it, which can be edited, liked, or added to a collection. Whether editing that prompt spends a credit is left unclear.

The evidence against it is that the items are presented as created by other people and link to creator profiles and followed accounts (O28, O30, O41); the evidence that would further separate the two is a feed item viewed with its creator's name and profile link shown.

tags.name: Group Membership
tags.rationale: Picsart represents spaces as distinct entities, each with space rules, bookmarked tools, and owners who created the space and can run challenges within it (O32). The user can join a space and leave it (O32). Under the decision ladder shared by Community Space, Group Membership and Clan / Guild, a surface takes the most specific level observed. Maintained membership, through join and leave, and governance, through owners and rules, are observed, while no group-owned state such as a group balance, total or rank is observed, so this label applies rather than either sibling. The entry's required condition that membership changes an observable product condition was not observed in operation: the session did not show what joining changes. Under the presence standard the product's own join and leave framing establishes presence, and the effect of membership is recorded as not observed, which is why the tag is held at strongly supported.
tags.alternativeConsidered: Community Space, which would apply if joining a space maintained no membership relationship that changes anything, leaving an open persistent context in which anyone contributes and interacts. The evidence that would separate them is a session comparing a space before and after joining, showing whether posting, entering the space challenge, feed content or notifications depend on membership.

observations.name: Spaces
observations.observed: Explore lists a large number of Spaces, each gathering a particular kind of creation under an owner who created it. A Space owner can start a challenge inside their own Space in addition to PicsArt's own challenges, and a Space challenge carries comments, likes and reactions. Every Space states its own rules and carries a set of bookmarked tools. A user can join a Space, share it, and leave it, and a Space's content and rules can be seen before joining. What joining actually changes, and whether joining requires approval, are left unclear.

tags.name: Challenge
tags.rationale: Picsart presents discrete challenge instances, each with a name, a type, rules, a countdown to the minute, and a stated prize (O24, O25). The success condition is winning, expressed as a prize of credits or a place in the winners' gallery, and concluded instances persist in a history listing winners from first to tenth place (O24, O27). The boundary is the countdown, and the product distinguishes winners from other entrants in that history (O25, O27). A separate voting stage with its own time limit sits between entry and history (O26). Space owners can also create challenges within their spaces (O32). Under the presence standard the implementation is recognizable from the product's own framing and from its concluded states. How winners are chosen, what happens after a submission, whether prizes are delivered automatically, and how a space challenge is bounded were not observed and are recorded as not observed.
tags.alternativeConsidered: A contest in which the product only ranks submissions without defining a challenge-level success condition, which the entry excludes. The evidence against it is that each instance states in advance a reward tied to winning and a deadline for entry (O24, O25); the evidence that would settle the success condition fully is a session carried through a challenge's close, showing how winners are determined and what non-winning entrants receive.

observations.name: Sister app promotion
observations.observed: The draw and color view features a separate drawing app, PicsArt Color, with an install prompt describing it as a full drawing suite for beginners and professionals. The promotion sits inside the Create surface beside PicsArt's own drawing tools.

observations.name: Invite friends and contacts
observations.observed: PicsArt offers to invite people by finding contacts or inviting friends directly by email, SMS or WhatsApp. Find contacts opens a system prompt asking to allow access to contacts. No reward for inviting is stated on the invite screen. Challenges, images and profiles can also be sent out as links through their own share controls.

observations.name: Project sharing controls
observations.observed: The editor's share-with option lets the user invite new people by email, shows who already has access and their role, and sets general access to view or restricted, alongside a copy-link option. Access is set per project, with a general access level plus named people. Roles beyond view are not listed.

observations.name: Save and export destinations
observations.observed: After saving, PicsArt offers to share the image, print it, send it in a message, or see more options, alongside sharing on PicsArt or in spaces. Export opens the same sharing options. Signing in through Apple, Google, Facebook or Snapchat links the PicsArt account to an identity held elsewhere.

observations.name: Try Pro paywall
observations.observed: The Try Pro button on the home screen opens the paywall again, this time with an easier-to-see close control. Its Pro tab promises increased access to AI-powered tools and premium content at the same prices as the first paywall. A Plus tab offers a starter set of premium tools not available on the free plan, at $1.25 a week yearly ($64.99 total) or $9.99 weekly, with the free trial available only on the yearly Plus plan. The Plus plan does not appear on the paywall shown right after sign-in. The Pro tab is shown first on opening. The same Pro and Plus pop-up also opens from Get more on the credits screen and from Apply on the Remove tool.

observations.name: Plan comparison table
observations.observed: Opening Learn more on a plan shows a comparison of Free, Plus and Pro, with Pro highlighted. It lists AI generation credits up to 200 on Plus and 500 on Pro, cloud storage of 5 GB on Plus and 100 GB on Pro, and multi-device premium access on 2 devices for Free, 5 for Plus and 10 for Pro. Pro includes every tool. The period the 200 and 500 credit figures apply to is not stated. The free profile's own allowance is 100 MB of storage and 5 weekly credits.

tags.name: Hard Currency
tags.rationale: The plan comparison lists credits for AI generation up to 200 on Plus and up to 500 on Pro, so a paid subscription adds units of the same product-defined credit (O38). The Get more control on the credits screen opens only the subscription offers (O22), and the Generate paywall headline is "Upgrade to get more credits" (O39). The credits screen also names add-on credits that do not expire (O20). No purchase was made, so the paid path is established from the product's plan copy rather than from a balance seen to increase, and the period over which plan credits apply was not stated (O38). The tag is held at strongly supported for that reason. This is a specialization of Spendable Credits and Tokens, noted as the parent; the same balance also carries Soft Currency.
tags.alternativeConsidered: A subscription that raises a usage limit without adding units to a stored balance, which would not be hard currency. The evidence against it is that the comparison and the paywall both name the benefit as credits, the same unit held and priced on the credits screen (O20, O21, O38, O39); the evidence that would settle it is a session on a paid plan showing the balance after subscribing, and how add-on credits are acquired.

observations.name: Credit-framed Generate paywall
observations.observed: The paywall opened by pressing Generate is headed around getting more credits to use with generative AI tools, and states at the bottom that cancellation is available any time before the next renewal. Neither the paid plans nor the free trial option state that PicsArt will send a reminder before renewal, and the paywall does not ask whether the user wants to be notified. Its headline names credits, while the Try Pro paywall names access to tools and content instead.

observations.name: Push prompt during export
observations.observed: While saving and exporting, PicsArt shows a pop-up promising to be first to try new features if push notifications are enabled, with a Stay updated button and an X. Tapping the X produces no stated effect.

observations.name: Notification bell
observations.observed: A notification bell sits in the top right corner of Discover. Tapping it opens the system prompt asking whether PicsArt can send notifications. The notification list showed PicsArt's own posted replays alongside what followed accounts are doing. The response given to the system prompt is not stated.

tags.name: Social Feed
tags.rationale: Discover opens a For you feed, described as never-ending, of images and videos created by other people (O30). Followed accounts' activity appears in the notification list beside a Picsart-posted item (O41), and creators are identifiable and followable from their content (O28). Explore adds AI Vibe items that disclose the prompt behind another creator's creation (O31). The items are attributed to multiple social actors and presented as a continuing stream for the viewer. The rule by which items are selected and ordered was not observed and is recorded as not observed.
tags.alternativeConsidered: A content recommendation surface without social attribution, which the entry excludes. The evidence against it is that the items are presented as created by other people and link to creator profiles and followed accounts (O28, O30, O41); the evidence that would further separate the two is a feed item viewed with its creator's name and profile link shown.

systemView: PicsArt is a medium system. Its spine is the AI-and-credit editing loop: opening the editor and asking for an AI result is what the free credit balance, the Pro and Plus subscriptions, and the two in-editor paywalls all hang from. A separate community layer of challenges, voting, creator profiles and Spaces runs alongside that spine and periodically pays back into the same credit balance through challenge prizes.

mechanicWriteups.name: Challenge
mechanicWriteups.summary: PicsArt runs bounded photo and video challenges with a minute-level countdown, a three-entry cap, a separate voting stage, and a persisted top-ten winners history.
mechanicWriteups.observed: PicsArt opens a dedicated challenges area from a cup icon in the navigation bar, split into active challenges, a voting stage and a history of past challenges. Each active challenge states its name, a countdown running down to the minute, and a prize, either a credit amount or a place in a winners' gallery. Entry is capped at three original submissions per user, and every submission is visible to other participants, 92 on one challenge at the time. A separate voting stage lets a user browse submissions and vote for more than one, with support shown after voting but no running vote count displayed anywhere. Concluded challenges move into a history that ranks winners from first to tenth place, and opening a winning entry shows its comments, its post date and how many hearts it received. Spaces, PicsArt's user-run interest groups, can also run their own challenges alongside PicsArt's own.
mechanicWriteups.presented: The challenges tab sits behind the cup-shaped navigation icon, with active challenges, voting and history as three separate sections. A challenge's own screen carries its countdown, rules, prize and entry control together, and a share control sends out a link to the challenge itself.
mechanicWriteups.noting: Prizes take two distinct forms inside the same mechanic, credits for some challenges and gallery placement for others, so the reward a user is chasing changes challenge to challenge even though the entry, voting and history structure stays the same. How winners are actually chosen is never stated on screen: the sequence of an entry stage, a separate voting stage, and a placed history points toward votes deciding placement, but editorial selection informed by votes would produce the exact same three screens.
findings: Active challenges state a name, a countdown to the minute, and a prize of either credits or gallery placement.
Entries are capped at three original submissions per challenge.
A separate voting stage lets a user support more than one submission, with no vote count shown.
Concluded challenges persist in a history ranking winners from first to tenth place.
Space owners can run their own challenges alongside PicsArt's own.
mechanicWriteups.screenshotsNote: the active challenges list with countdown and prize, and the challenge history screen showing ranked winners.

mechanicWriteups.name: Leaderboard
mechanicWriteups.summary: PicsArt's only ranking is the first-to-tenth winners list attached to each concluded challenge, with no stated measure behind the order.
mechanicWriteups.observed: PicsArt's challenge history lists winners of past challenges in order from first to tenth place. Opening a winning entry shows its comments, its post date, and the number of hearts it received, but nothing on screen states what decided the order. Neither browsing submissions nor voting on a challenge in progress shows a running vote count to anyone.
mechanicWriteups.presented: The ranking appears only inside challenge history, reached from the same cup-icon area as active challenges and voting, with each past challenge opening its own first-to-tenth list.
mechanicWriteups.noting: The ordering itself is stated plainly, first through tenth, but PicsArt never states what produces it. The three-stage structure, entry, then voting with rewards shown, then a placed history, points toward votes deciding the order, but the same three screens would look identical if PicsArt selected winners editorially and framed the result the same way.
findings: Challenge history ranks winners in order from first to tenth place.
A winning entry shows its comments, post date and heart count.
No running vote count is shown anywhere during voting.
What decides placement is never stated on screen.
mechanicWriteups.screenshotsNote: the challenge history list ranking winners first to tenth, and an opened winning entry showing its comments and hearts.

mechanicWriteups.name: Social Feed
mechanicWriteups.summary: Every item in PicsArt's Discover feed carries a Try control that opens the exact tool or effect used to make it, applied to the viewer's own material.
mechanicWriteups.observed: PicsArt's Discover section opens on a For You feed, described as never-ending, made up of images and videos from other creators. Every item shows a before and after and carries a Try control letting the user apply the same tool, effect or generation to their own material. The notification list surfaces activity from accounts the user follows alongside PicsArt's own posts. Explore adds an AI Vibe section where pressing and holding an item reveals the prompt used to create it, which the user can edit, like, or add to a collection.
mechanicWriteups.presented: Discover and Explore are separate tabs in the main navigation. Feed items carry the Try control directly on the item rather than behind a menu, and AI Vibe's prompt disclosure appears only on a press and hold rather than at a glance.
mechanicWriteups.noting: The feed is built to be acted on rather than only viewed. A Try control on every item turns each post into an entry point for the specific tool that produced it, and AI Vibe goes further by showing the exact prompt behind someone else's generation rather than only the result. Neither the ordering rule for the For You feed nor what Try actually opens is named.
findings: The For You feed is described as never-ending and made up of other creators' images and videos.
Every feed item carries a Try control and a before-and-after view.
Followed accounts' activity appears in the notification list.
AI Vibe discloses the prompt behind another creator's generation and lets the viewer edit it.
mechanicWriteups.screenshotsNote: a Discover feed item showing its Try control and before-and-after, and an AI Vibe item with its disclosed prompt.

mechanicWriteups.name: Group Membership
mechanicWriteups.summary: PicsArt's Spaces are joinable, owner-run groups with their own rules and bookmarked tools, but nothing changes for a user once they actually join one.
mechanicWriteups.observed: PicsArt's Explore area lists Spaces, each gathering a particular kind of creation under an owner who created it. Every Space carries its own stated rules and a set of bookmarked tools, and a Space owner can start a challenge inside their Space in addition to PicsArt's own challenges. A user can join a Space, share it, and leave it, and a Space's content and rules can be seen before joining.
mechanicWriteups.presented: Spaces sit inside Explore alongside categories, brand content and templates, each with its own join and leave controls and a challenge shown alongside PicsArt's own challenges.
mechanicWriteups.noting: PicsArt shows everything a Space offers, its content, its rules, its challenges, before asking anyone to join it. Membership is tracked through join and leave rather than left open to anyone, and Spaces are run by identified owners rather than the product itself, but what that membership actually changes, whether feed content, posting rights or notifications, is never stated.
findings: Spaces are owned and created by users, each with its own stated rules.
A Space owner can run a challenge inside their own Space.
Joining and leaving a Space are both single controls.
A Space's content and rules can be seen before joining.
mechanicWriteups.screenshotsNote: the Explore list of Spaces, and a single Space showing its rules, bookmarked tools and join control.

mechanicWriteups.name: Soft Currency
mechanicWriteups.summary: PicsArt prices each AI tool's specific output in credits drawn from a weekly-renewing free balance, letting the user choose which result to spend on rather than draining a shared capacity.
mechanicWriteups.observed: PicsArt shows a credit balance on the user's profile, 5 credits on a free account, and a credits screen explains that the plan includes weekly credits that renew every six days. The same screen prices each kind of AI result separately: one credit for an AI sticker, two for tools like AI logo generator or AI writer, three for any filter, four for tools like AI background or AI image editor, and fifty for an AI avatar. Add-on credits are named separately as not expiring, distinct from the renewing weekly allowance. Challenges also pay their prizes in credits, and the challenge and subscription copy both frame credits as what makes generative AI tools accessible.
mechanicWriteups.presented: The balance sits on the profile screen and opens into a dedicated credits screen from Learn more, which lists every tool's price in one table. The same figure reappears as the prize amount on challenge cards.
mechanicWriteups.noting: PicsArt's credits behave as a currency spent across differently priced results rather than as a depleting capacity for repeated use of one tool. Each AI tool carries its own fixed price, from one credit to fifty, so the balance is something the user allocates among several possible outputs rather than a meter that runs out the more a single feature is used. Nothing in the credits screen or the AI panel ties a credit cost to attempts, retries or time; it is tied to which specific tool and result the user chooses. That is what separates this from an Energy system: PicsArt sells priced results to pick among, not a capacity that depletes with use.
findings: A free profile holds 5 credits that renew weekly, on a six-day cycle.
Individual AI results are priced separately, from 1 credit for an AI sticker up to 50 for an AI avatar.
Add-on credits are described as not expiring, distinct from the renewing weekly allowance.
Challenges pay prizes in the same credits, as much as 50 for a single win.
mechanicWriteups.screenshotsNote: the profile screen showing the credit balance, and the credits screen listing per-tool prices.

mechanicWriteups.name: Hard Currency
mechanicWriteups.summary: The only way to raise PicsArt's credit balance beyond its weekly free allowance is buying a Pro or Plus subscription, sold explicitly in terms of credits rather than tools.
mechanicWriteups.observed: The Get more control on the credits screen opens only a choice between Pro and Plus, with no way to buy credits on their own. The plan comparison lists AI generation credits up to 200 on Plus and up to 500 on Pro, alongside separate cloud storage and device allowances. The paywall reached from the Generate button is headed around getting more credits and states that access can be cancelled any time before the next renewal.
mechanicWriteups.presented: The upgrade path from Get more, from the Generate paywall, and from Try Pro all lead to the same Pro and Plus comparison, each naming credits as part of what a subscription buys.
mechanicWriteups.noting: PicsArt sells the same subscription two different ways depending on where the offer appears. The Try Pro entry point on the home screen frames the purchase around tools and content, while the paywall reached by pressing Generate on an AI model frames the identical purchase around credits. Both open the same Pro and Plus choice, so the difference is in what each entry point calls the thing being bought, not in what is actually offered.
findings: No standalone credit purchase exists; only Pro and Plus subscriptions add to the balance.
Plus lists up to 200 AI generation credits and Pro up to 500.
The Generate paywall names credits as the benefit; the Try Pro paywall names tools and content.
Cancellation is stated as available any time before the next renewal.
mechanicWriteups.screenshotsNote:
the Get more pop-up offering Pro or Plus, and the plan comparison table showing credit allowances.

sectionLeadIns.social: PicsArt's social layer runs on challenges with voting and a winners' history, creator profiles and following, joinable Spaces, and a feed built from other people's work.

proposedTags.name: Try This Look
proposedTags.draftDefinition: A reuse prompt attaches to a creation attributed to another actor, shown in a browsing surface, a control that applies the same effect, template, tool or generation settings to the viewer's own material, and presents the creation with what produced it, such as a before and after pair or the prompt used. The subject of the control is the method behind someone else's creation, and its destination is the viewer's own creating.
proposedTags.conditions: A feed or gallery of creations attributed to other actors; a control on the individual item rather than on the surface; disclosure of how the item was made, as a before and after view or a visible prompt; and a route from that control into the product's creation tools applied to the viewer's material.
proposedTags.whyNotCovered: Social Feed classifies the stream of socially attributed items but not a per-item route that converts viewing into the viewer's own creation. Shareable Win covers representations of accomplishments sent outward, and excludes the user's own work. Community Space and Group Membership cover shared contexts rather than reuse of another creator's method. No approved entry classifies the conversion of browsing someone else's output into a start on one's own.
proposedTags.recurrenceElsewhere: Expected in creative, design and short-video products, where a control on another person's post applies the same effect, template or settings to the viewer's own material (tier: plausible, not yet observed in a second analyzed app). No second app carrying this shape has been recorded in this library.
proposedTags.caveat: Held as an open proposal on 16 Sep 2026. The Try control was never tapped and the AI Vibe prompt was never run (O30, O31). What is unobserved is the substance of the mechanic rather than a detail around it: where the control leads, whether the viewer's own material is loaded into it, and whether reuse costs credits or requires Pro. Two pieces of evidence would settle the proposal. The first is a Picsart session that taps Try on a feed item and follows it through to a finished result, recording the screen it opens, what material is loaded, and any credit deduction or paywall met on the way. The second is a walkthrough of another app carrying the same shape: a control on another person's creation that applies the same method to the viewer's own material. Until both exist, the proposal stays open and is not written as an entry.

system.tagline: A creative platform whose only two entry points into the paid economy sit inside the same editor, one before a result exists and one after.
system.overview: PicsArt's spine is the AI-and-credit editing loop: opening the editor and asking for an AI result is what the free credit balance, the Pro and Plus subscriptions, and two separately placed paywalls all hang from. A community layer, challenges with a countdown and a separate voting stage, creator profiles, and joinable Spaces, runs alongside that spine and periodically pays back into the same credit balance through challenge prizes.
system.loop: The core loop is: open the Create surface → start an edit or open the AI panel → press Generate on a premium model, which opens a paywall before any result exists, or try the Pro-marked Remove tool, which opens a paywall only at Apply, after the tool has been tried → save or export. A free profile's weekly credit allowance prices each AI result separately, and a Pro or Plus subscription is the only way to raise it. Challenges take entries, run a separate voting stage, and pay some winners in the same credits and others in gallery placement, and a Space owner can run a challenge inside their own Space.
system.keyInsight: PicsArt places its purchase request at two different points inside the same editor: at Generate on the AI models, before any result exists, and at Apply on the Remove tool, after the tool has already been tried. Both open the identical Pro and Plus choice, so the difference is entirely in when and how each request is framed, not in what is being sold.
system.whatMakesItWork: The credit balance is what ties the editor to the community layer without either side needing to know much about the other: challenge prizes and subscription upgrades both land in the same balance the editor already prices its tools against, so a win in the community layer and a purchase in the monetization layer both cash out as the same currency spent the same way.

roles.role: Bounded challenge instances with a minute-level countdown, a three-entry cap, and a prize of either credits or gallery placement, concluding into a first-to-tenth winners history.
Challenge history ranks winners first to tenth for each concluded challenge, with no stated measure behind the order beyond the entry, voting and history sequence itself.
A never-ending Discover feed of other creators' work where every item carries a Try control that opens the exact tool or effect used to make it, applied to the viewer's own material.
Joinable, owner-run Spaces with their own stated rules and bookmarked tools; a Space owner can run a challenge inside their own Space, but nothing else changes once a user joins.

A weekly-renewing free credit balance priced separately against each AI tool, from 1 credit for a sticker to 50 for an avatar, so the user chooses among priced results rather than draining a depleting capacity.

The only route to more credits than the free weekly allowance is a Pro or Plus subscription, sold in terms of credits on the paywall reached from Generate and in terms of tools and content on the paywall reached from Try Pro.

connections.title: A Space owner can run their own challenge
connections.desc: A user who owns a Space can start a challenge inside it, in addition to PicsArt's own challenges.
connections.effect: Space membership isn't only a feed to browse, an owner can turn their own Space into a second source of challenge entries.

connections.title: A concluded challenge becomes a ranked history
connections.desc: Challenge history turns each concluded challenge into a ranked list of winners from first to tenth place.
connections.effect: The only ranking PicsArt shows anywhere is downstream of a challenge actually finishing, not a standing measure kept on its own.

connections.title: Challenge prizes pay into the same credit balance
connections.desc: Some challenges pay their prize in credits, the identical balance the editor prices its AI tools against.
connections.effect: Winning a challenge and generating an AI result draw on and add to the same number, tying the community side of the app to the economy the editor runs on.

connections.title: A subscription adds to the same balance it doesn't replace
connections.desc: Pro and Plus raise the credit balance to 500 or 200 respectively, on top of the same weekly allowance a free account already has.
connections.effect: Paying doesn't open a separate premium currency, it just adds more of the identical credits a free user already spends.
